opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the more interesting trade-offs in hybrid attention design. When you mix a small number of full-attention layers with many linear or sliding-window layers, the full-attention layers carry most of the long-context cost: their KV cache grows with sequence length, and their compute grows quadratically during prefill. The other layers stay roughly constant in memory, or linear in compute.

So if you scale the model up, mostly by making it deeper or wider in the efficient layers, and you keep the number of full-attention layers fixed rather than scaling them proportionally, the share of the model that pays the long-context cost actually shrinks. The KV cache per token grows much more slowly than total parameters, and at 128K or longer you feel that directly in throughput and in how many requests you can batch.

The open question is whether quality holds. The full-attention layers act as global retrieval points, where the model can look back precisely at any earlier token. Our intuition, and what we've seen so far, is that you don't need that capability in every layer. You need it at a few well-placed points, and the rest of the network can do local or compressed processing. A larger model also seems better at using those few global layers, because the intermediate representations are richer, so each lookup is more informative.

It isn't free, though. If the ratio gets too extreme, you start seeing weaknesses on tasks that need many-hop retrieval across a long context, or exact copying from far back. So in practice we watch long-context benchmarks closely, not just the usual short ones, and look for the point where adding efficiency stops costing capability. But broadly, keeping full attention fixed while scaling everything else is one of the more promising ways to make long context cheap at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says full-attention layers carry much of the long-context cost, but does not clearly state that adding more such layers increases that cost.

r002.rationale: It says fixed full-attention layers can make scaling more efficient, but does not compare Pro with Flash or say Pro retains roughly Flash’s long-context efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually one of the key design decisions we spent a lot of time on. The intuition is fairly simple: when you scale a model up, if you keep the number of full-attention layers fixed rather than scaling them proportionally with depth, the fraction of the model that pays the full quadratic cost in sequence length keeps shrinking. So the larger model becomes relatively more efficient on long contexts, not less. Most of the depth you add is made up of cheaper layers, whether that's sliding-window attention or a linear or recurrent mechanism, and those scale essentially linearly with context length.

What that means in practice is that the KV cache, which is really the bottleneck for long-context inference, grows with the number of full-attention layers rather than with total depth. If you have, say, a handful of global layers in a model with a hundred layers, your memory footprint for a very long context is a small fraction of what a pure transformer of the same size would need. That lets you serve longer contexts at the same batch size, or more concurrent users at the same context, which is where the real cost lives.

The question people always ask is whether you lose quality. Our experience is that a small number of full-attention layers is enough to do the global information routing, the retrieval across the whole context, as long as they are placed well and the intermediate layers can carry the local structure. The larger model actually has more capacity to make use of those few global layers, so the gap to a full-attention baseline tends to close as you scale, rather than widen. Where you do have to be careful is with tasks that need very dense long-range dependencies, like certain forms of multi-hop retrieval, and that's where we spend most of our evaluation effort now.

r001.rationale: The response says the KV cache grows with the number of full-attention layers and that those layers incur the full quadratic sequence-length cost, so adding such layers increases long-context costs.

r002.rationale: It says larger models become relatively more efficient when the number of full-attention layers stays fixed, but it does not identify Pro or compare its efficiency with Flash.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that, as the model gets deeper, you don’t have to increase the number of full-attention layers proportionally. Full attention is particularly expensive at long context lengths, so keeping that number fixed can help keep its share of the total cost under control. If the additional layers use a more efficient attention mechanism, you can scale model capacity without scaling the most expensive long-context computation at the same rate.

But that doesn’t make long context free. Those full-attention layers still have quadratic attention computation as the sequence grows, and the other layers still add cost. The important question is whether a fixed number of layers can provide enough global information exchange as the model gets larger. You’d want to test that on tasks requiring reasoning across distant parts of the context, alongside measuring memory use and latency.

r001.rationale: The response says full attention is particularly expensive at long context lengths and that increasing its layer count with model depth would scale that computation; keeping the count fixed helps control the cost.

r002.rationale: The response says capacity can grow without scaling the most expensive computation at the same rate, but it does not compare Pro with Flash or say their long-text processing efficiency stays roughly the same.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that, as the model gets larger, you don’t necessarily need to increase the number of full-attention layers along with its depth. You can keep a fixed number of layers for global interaction and use more efficient attention in the remaining layers. That way, the most expensive long-context computation doesn’t grow proportionally with the total number of layers.

It doesn’t eliminate the quadratic cost of those full-attention layers, but it can reduce their share of the overall computation and the KV cache substantially. The question is whether those few layers provide enough global information exchange to preserve quality. If they do, the efficiency advantage can become more significant as the model grows.

r001.rationale: The response says full-attention layers carry the expensive long-context computation and that their quadratic cost grows with their number.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Pro or Flash, or claim that Pro can retain roughly Flash’s efficiency as parameter count increases with a fixed number of full-attention layers.
